solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Breeding establishment for Spooner — and for us!

definitions.note: loosely: bloodstock is what a stud breeds, so the phrase serves as a definition for us too

indicators.note: Dr Spooner famously swapped the opening sounds of neighbouring words, so the phrase must be said his way

blocks.note: a breeding establishment is a stud block; swap the opening sounds of the two words

explanation.surface: A horse-breeding farm is described in a way that suits both the famous word-muddler and ordinary folk.
explanation.walkthrough: STUD BLOCK with its opening sounds swapped is BLUD STOCK, i.e. BLOODSTOCK; 'and for us' says the unswapped phrase also points at the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Thoroughbred horses kept for breeding are called bloodstock, which is exactly what a stud farm houses and produces.

clue.text: Darling Ruth?

blocks.note: first meaning: an affectionate term for a loved one
second meaning: the nickname of the American baseball star George Herman Ruth

explanation.walkthrough: Read together the words look like addressing someone called Ruth fondly; the question mark flags that Ruth is a definition by example, the baseball player Babe Ruth.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is a term of endearment and also the famous nickname carried by baseball legend Ruth.

clue.text: Concerning East Anglian feature, this writer has to be rude

blocks.note: of means about or concerning
the Fens are the flat marshy lowlands of eastern England
the setter saying 'I have', contracted

explanation.surface: A writer finds that talking about some East Anglian landmark obliges them to be impolite.
explanation.walkthrough: 'This writer' is the setter, so 'this writer has' is I'VE with the apostrophe dropped. The Fens are low-lying drained marshland in East Anglia.
explanation.definitionFit: Something offensive causes insult or upset, the same sense as rude remarks or behaviour.

clue.text: Follow mother’s unquestioning belief?

blocks.note: to dog someone is to follow them closely
a familiar word for mother

explanation.surface: A child is urged to accept whatever their mother believes without question.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Follow' reads as an instruction to obey mother, but it is the verb meaning to trail someone.
explanation.definitionFit: A dogma is a principle laid down as unquestionably true, a creed held without doubt.

clue.text: Fix article of clothing not properly done up?

definitions.text: article of clothing not properly done up?

blocks.note: first meaning: to secure something firmly in place

blocks.clueFragment: article of clothing not properly done up?
blocks.note: second meaning, whimsical: a neckwear item left hanging loose rather than knotted up at the collar

explanation.surface: Someone is told to sort out a garment that has been fastened carelessly.
explanation.walkthrough: The second half is a playful description: a necktie that is down rather than done up; the question mark warns of the stretch.
explanation.definitionFit: To tie down a load is to fasten it securely, which is one sense of the verb fix.

clue.text: Danced in item of clothing provocatively coloured?

blocks.note: a cape is a sleeveless cloak
red is the colour that provokes, as a red rag to a bull

explanation.surface: Someone dances about in a garment of a daring, attention-seeking colour.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In' looks like it describes what the dancer wore, but it only links the definition to the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: To caper is to skip or leap about playfully, which is a lively kind of dancing.

clue.text: Illustrious man and very important lady in house

indicators.note: one thing being in another means it sits inside it

blocks.note: ER is the Queen, Elizabeth Regina
HO is the abbreviation for house

explanation.surface: A distinguished gentleman and a grand lady share a home.
explanation.walkthrough: ER, the royal cipher of Elizabeth Regina, is the crossword's standard queen; HO is a standard abbreviation for house.
explanation.definitionFit: A hero is a man admired for courage or great deeds, so famous and illustrious.

clue.text: Poet and priest with holy books

blocks.note: Eli is the priest who raised Samuel in the Old Testament
joins the two pieces
OT is the Old Testament

explanation.surface: A poet and a clergyman sit together with scripture.
explanation.walkthrough: Eli is the crossword's usual priest, from the Books of Samuel; OT stands for the Old Testament.
explanation.definitionFit: T. S. Eliot, author of The Waste Land, is one of the best-known twentieth-century poets writing in English.

clue.text: Dominant, ruling part of Yorkshire once

blocks.note: to be over others is to be in charge of them
Yorkshire was divided into three Ridings until 1974

explanation.surface: A historic district of Yorkshire is described as holding sway over the rest.
explanation.walkthrough: The Ridings (North, East and West) were Yorkshire's old administrative divisions.
explanation.definitionFit: An overriding concern is one more important than any other, so dominant or paramount.

clue.text: After accident large tin is intact

indicators.note: an accident leaves things smashed and jumbled, so the letters are thrown into a new order

blocks.note: the letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: After a crash, a big can has somehow come through undamaged.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface says the tin survived the accident; in fact the accident is what wrecks its letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Integral can mean whole and complete, with nothing missing, the same sense as intact.

clue.text: Obscure English female hides in lavatory, rather rudely

indicators.note: someone who hides in a place is enclosed by it, so one piece goes inside another

blocks.note: E is the abbreviation for English
F is the abbreviation for female
bog is coarse British slang for a toilet

explanation.surface: An Englishwoman takes refuge in the toilet, described in rather crude terms.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rather rudely' tells you the lavatory word is a vulgar one: bog is British slang for a toilet.
explanation.definitionFit: To befog is to cloud or confuse something, making it unclear, which is what obscuring does.

clue.text: Dear old lover musing

blocks.note: an ex is a former partner
pensive means lost in thought

explanation.surface: Someone thinks wistfully about a beloved former sweetheart.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dear' reads as an endearment for the old lover, but it is the definition in its sense of costly.
explanation.definitionFit: Dear in British usage also means high-priced, so a dear item costs a lot of money.

clue.text: Where you see a five relative to four well thought of!

indicators.note: asking where something is found invites the reply that it sits inside another word

blocks.note: the answer to 'where' is the position word itself
taken as written
V is the Roman numeral for five
the number word, spelt out

explanation.surface: A question about where a five might appear in relation to a four.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer is a statement of position: A V is IN F-OUR, which spells IN F(AV)OUR.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone in favour enjoys approval or popularity, so they are regarded highly by others.

clue.text: Chemical destroying trees

indicators.note: whatever is destroyed is broken apart, so these letters are rebuilt in another order

blocks.note: the letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: Some toxic substance is killing off the woodland.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface pictures a pollutant killing trees; 'destroying' is the signal to rearrange them.
explanation.definitionFit: An ester is an organic compound formed from an acid and an alcohol, a specific chemical substance.

clue.text: Associate comic with place that’s funny

indicators.note: funny here means peculiar or odd, so the letters come out in a strange order

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A comedian is linked with a venue that makes people laugh.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Funny' sits naturally beside 'comic', but it means odd here and signals the rearrangement.
explanation.definitionFit: An accomplice is a partner who helps another in wrongdoing, a criminal associate.

clue.text: Smart little boy’s menu option?

blocks.note: chic means stylish
Ken is the short form of the boy's name Kenneth

explanation.surface: A clever young lad chooses something from the restaurant menu.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Little boy' means a short boy's name, not a child; the question mark marks the definition as one example of a menu choice.
explanation.definitionFit: Chicken is a common dish offered in restaurants, one example of an item to order.

clue.text: King established calm in part of Lincolnshire once

blocks.note: K is the chess abbreviation for king
EST is the abbreviation for established, as on shop signs
even means steady or unruffled

explanation.surface: A monarch restored peace in a district of an eastern English county long ago.
explanation.walkthrough: Lincolnshire was historically split into three Parts: Lindsey, Holland and Kesteven; 'in' only links.
explanation.definitionFit: Kesteven was one of the three historic administrative Parts into which the county of Lincolnshire was divided.

clue.text: Some made dire decision — about to be mocked

indicators.note: some of a phrase is only a portion of it, so the letters are a run within the words
to turn about is to face the other way, so the run is read backwards

blocks.note: the run of letters from the end of the first word to the start of the third

explanation.surface: Someone made a terrible choice and is about to be ridiculed for it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'About to be' reads as 'going to be', but 'about' is the reversal signal and 'to be' the link.
explanation.definitionFit: To deride someone is to laugh at them with contempt, which is the same as mocking.

clue.text: County’s side in an undesirable financial situation

blocks.note: County Down in Northern Ireland, with the possessive S
a wing is one side of a building or team

explanation.surface: A county's sports team finds itself in financial trouble.
explanation.walkthrough: County Down is one of the six counties of Northern Ireland; its possessive gives DOWN'S.
explanation.definitionFit: A downswing is a downward trend in business or the economy, a worrying slump for finances.

clue.text: Discloses writers brought in by university press

indicators.note: what is brought in by something ends up inside it

blocks.note: OUP is Oxford University Press
pens are writing implements

explanation.surface: A university publisher signs up new authors and reveals something.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Writers' suggests authors, but here they are the implements used to write; OUP is Oxford University Press.
explanation.definitionFit: To open up is to speak frankly and reveal information, which is what disclosing means.

clue.text: Webfooted pair of chums

indicators.note: a pair means two of something, so two separate words are wanted side by side

blocks.note: a pal is a friend
a mate is a friend, in British usage

explanation.surface: Two friends who happen to have webbed feet, like a couple of ducks.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pair of chums' asks for two synonyms of chum set side by side.
explanation.definitionFit: Palmate describes a hand-shaped structure, and in zoology birds with webbed toes such as ducks.

clue.text: PM‘s obvious victory

blocks.note: a bald statement is plain and undisguised
a win is a victory

explanation.surface: A Prime Minister wins an election by a clear margin.
explanation.walkthrough: Stanley Baldwin was the Conservative British Prime Minister three times between the wars.
explanation.definitionFit: Stanley Baldwin served as Prime Minister of the United Kingdom in the 1920s and 1930s.

clue.text: Large old rocker appears to be intolerant

blocks.note: big means large
O is the abbreviation for old
a Ted, or Teddy boy, was a 1950s British youth devoted to rock and roll

explanation.surface: An ageing, overweight rock musician seems narrow-minded.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Old rocker' suggests an aged rock star; instead O is old and a Ted is a 1950s Teddy boy, a British rock-and-roll fan in Edwardian-style suits.
explanation.definitionFit: A bigoted person holds prejudiced views and refuses to accept others' opinions, so is intolerant.

clue.text: Insert text from F onwards?

blocks.note: first meaning: to put copied text into a document
second meaning, split in two: every letter from F on comes after E in the alphabet

explanation.surface: An instruction to put text into a document starting at the letter F.
explanation.walkthrough: Read the answer as PAST E: F and every letter after it lie past E; the question mark flags the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: In computing, to paste is to put previously copied or cut text into a document.

clue.text: A yen at the end of a day for exotic dish

indicators.note: coming at the end means being placed after something else in the line

blocks.note: Sat is the abbreviation for Saturday
taken as written
Y is the symbol for the Japanese yen

explanation.surface: At the close of the day someone craves some foreign food.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Yen' looks like a craving, fitting the surface, but it is the Japanese currency, abbreviated Y.
explanation.definitionFit: Satay is a Southeast Asian dish of grilled skewered meat with peanut sauce, foreign to British tables.

clue.text: Member of the elite class strictly adhering to regulations

definitions.note: the answer is a noun for a person who does this

blocks.note: a limb, one of the body's members
the A-list is the top tier of celebrities

explanation.surface: A snob from the upper class who sticks rigidly to the rules.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Member of the elite' reads as one person; split it: a member is a limb, and the elite class is the A-list.
explanation.definitionFit: A legalist insists on literal observance of laws and rules, being rigid about regulations.

clue.text: The first woman to occupy a position in the French bank

indicators.note: to occupy a spot within something is to sit inside it

blocks.note: le is French for the
Eve is the first woman in Genesis

explanation.surface: A pioneering woman becomes the first to hold a post in a French bank.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bank' suggests finance, reinforced by 'the French bank'; it is a riverbank, and 'the French' is just LE.
explanation.definitionFit: A levee is an embankment built along a river to prevent flooding, a kind of bank.

clue.text: Some that may be walking in units

blocks.note: first meaning: the parts of the body used for walking
second meaning: units of length, twelve inches each

explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a group walking in formation; 'in' simply joins two meanings of one word.
explanation.definitionFit: The body parts at the end of the legs share their name with an imperial measure of length.

clue.text: Having trouble as traveller occupying vehicle towed by tractor?

definitions.text: as traveller occupying vehicle towed by tractor?

blocks.note: first meaning: a British idiom for being in a difficult situation

blocks.clueFragment: as traveller occupying vehicle towed by tractor?
blocks.note: second meaning, literal: riding in a trailer pulled behind farm machinery

explanation.surface: A passenger has a bumpy time riding in a trailer behind a tractor.
explanation.walkthrough: The British idiom for being in a fix is taken literally in the second half; the question mark flags the whimsy.
explanation.definitionFit: The informal British phrase means being in serious difficulty or in a predicament.

clue.text: Fabric not at all nice with hole in it

indicators.note: having something with it here means holding it within

blocks.note: vile means thoroughly unpleasant
the letter O is shaped like a hole

explanation.surface: Some unpleasant cloth has a hole in it.
explanation.walkthrough: A letter O looks like a hole, a crossword staple; it goes inside the word for nasty.
explanation.definitionFit: Voile is a thin, semi-transparent cotton or silk material used for curtains and dresses.

clue.text: Irish singer always coming back to entertain any number

indicators.note: coming back means travelling the opposite way, so the letters run backwards
to entertain guests is to take them in, so one piece holds another

blocks.note: aye is an old word for always, ever
N stands for an unspecified number in mathematics

explanation.surface: An Irish performer keeps returning to sing for crowds of any size.
explanation.walkthrough: Aye, meaning always (as in 'for aye'), rhymes with day, not eye.
explanation.definitionFit: Enya is the Irish singer-songwriter famous for the atmospheric hit Orinoco Flow.

clue.text: A widget he’d constructed — something hard to carry around?

indicators.note: what is constructed is assembled from parts, so the letters are built into a new order

blocks.note: the letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: Someone has built a gadget so bulky it is a burden to lug about.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface's gadget really would be heavy; 'constructed' is the rearrangement signal.
explanation.definitionFit: A dead weight is an inert, heavy load that is difficult to lift or move.
